A Conceptual Framework for a Real-Time, Deep 
Learning Model to Estimate In vitro Chewing Cycles 
Required for Safe Swallowing 
 
Isurie Akarawita, Bangxiang  Chen, Jaspreet Dhupia, Weiliang Xu  
Dept. of Mechanical and Mechatronics Engineering 
The University of Auckland 
Auckland, New Zealand 
iaka416@aucklanduni.ac.nz 
 
Martin Stommel 
Dept. of Electrical and Electronic Engineering 
Auckland University of Technology 
Auckland, New Zealand 
mstommel@aut.ac.nz
Abstract— Research on chewing robots is crucial for 
understanding and improving the mechanical process of food 
breakdown, helping to better replicate the human oral system . 
This study presents a novel conceptu al framework for a machine 
vision and deep learning model that predicts the number of 
chewing cycles a robot needs to form a safe and swallowable bolus 
in real time, providing valuable insights into oral food breakdown. 
Utilizing image -based data acquisition and advanced deep 
learning algorithms, this model proposes a  real-time in vitro 
chewing behavior analysis compared to existing robots. The 
methodology involves  capturing chewing behavior through 
machine vision, data preprocessing, designing and training a deep 
learning model on time-invariant and time-variant variables, and 
optimizing for real -time predictions. The framework seeks to 
revolutionize the analysis of in vitro mastication processes, holding 
significant promise for various fields, including optimizing food 
product development, evaluating dental materials, and improving 
oral health products.  
Keywords—Deep learning , machine vision, chewing cycles, 
invitro, image processing 
I. INTRODUCTION 
In an era where components replicating specific human 
functions are increasingly manufactured, chewing robots have 
become a significant area of development [1  - 2 ]. A chewing 
robot is a device designed to replicate the mechanical processes 
of human chewing, helping to study and improve oral food 
processing. The goal for a chewing robot is to replicate human 
oral processing of food accurately.

A chewing 
robot is a device designed to replicate the mechanical processes 
of human chewing, helping to study and improve oral food 
processing. The goal for a chewing robot is to replicate human 
oral processing of food accurately. It forms a chewed food bolus 
by mechanically breaking down food through repeated chewing 
cycles. The number of chewing cycles is relevant because it 
directly impacts the consistency and safety of the bolus, which 
must be adequately broken down to be considered safe for 
swallowing. Safety, in this context, is defined as the ability of 
the bolus to be swallowed without causing choking or 
discomfort, ensuring it mimics human oral processing as closely 
as possible. One such research is where a chewing robot has 
been developed with compliance control to adapt chewing 
velocity based on food texture force profiles derived using a 
Texture Profile Analyzer (TPA) [ 1]. Also, the effec tiveness of 
robotic chewing is evaluated by measuring the particle size 
distributions (PSDs) and median size diameters of chewed 
peanuts extracted out from the robotic oral cavity [3].  
Some researchers have focused solely on mimicking jaw 
movements, such as the 6PUS -2HKP (6 prismatic -universal-
spherical chains, 2 higher kinematic pairs) robot. It is a 
redundantly actuated parallel robot (RAPR) based on 
musculoskeletal biomechanics [ 4]. Additionally, a novel 
humanoid chewing robot replicates human chewing motions in 
a controlled environment, incorporating artificial saliva and 
measuring xylitol release from gum using xylitol enzymatic kit 
and a UV-Vis spectrophotometer [5]. In another research, food 
masses have been collected in coffee filters, and scanned using 
a flatbed scanner to determine, the median particle size [ 6]. 
Moreover, the physical properties such as the texture of the food 
bolus are tested using instrumental TPA, and food bolus particle 
sizes are evaluated via sieving [7].

Moreover, the physical properties such as the texture of the food

introduced into the robot's oral cavity or after the chewing 
process has been completed.  
A recent chewing robot for food research simulates human 
chewing with bi -directional movements. It evaluates chewing 
using real -time sensors for texture, conductivity, pH, and 
temperature. However, this method depends on traditional 
mechanical and sensor -based techniques  [8]. Furthermore, 
achieving a safe, swallowable bolus comparable to that formed 
by humans would be a major milestone [ 9]. However, despite 
advancements in chewing robot technology, when a bite- sized 
portion of food is introduced in an in vitro oral cavity, accurately 
replicating the safe swallowable bolus remains unaccomplished 
[10]. Therefore, it is clear that this is an emerging research area 
with substantial untapped potential. 
Hence, this study proposes a conceptual framework for a 
real-time deep learning model to estimate the additional in vitro 
chewing cycles needed for safe bolus formation. This model will 
be integrated with existing robotic oral cavity [ 3] with the aim 
to create an intelligent system  that closely mimics human oral 
processing. By correlating various inputs with bolus dynamics 
using advanced machine learning, we seek to develop a model 
that accurately predicts the necessary chewing cycles for a safe, 
swallowable bolus. Each section of this paper details 
components of the conceptual model, offering a comprehensive 
overview.

II. PROPOSED FRAMEWORK 
The framework integrates a chewing robot, machine vision 
for data acquisition, and deep learning algorithms for real -time 
analysis as in Figure 1. Prediction of chewing cycles is crucial  
as it directly affects the consistency and safety of the bolus, 
ensuring it is  adequately broken down to closely resemble a 
human-chewed food bolus.

III. IN VITRO CHEWING ROBOT SYSTEM SETUP 
A. Chewing Robot 
The chewing robot used in this study, is designed to simulate 
human chewing patterns with high precision, providing 
consistent and reliable data for analysis as explained in [3]. The 
robot simulates the molar crushing and grinding during chewing 
by generating different trajectories. A silicon rubber oral cavity 
mimics the soft tissue surrounding the lower molar, containing 
and repositioning the food between occlusions through 
pneumatic bellows. Chewing parameters, including molar 
trajectories and saliva flo w rate, are adjustable in the robot to 
examine their effects on the food. The robot's saliva injection 
rate is controlled by an automatic syringe.  
B. Vision System 
The vision system is crucial for the Machine Vision and 
Deep Learning Model, enabling real -time assessment and 
prediction of in vitro chewing behavior. Advanced imaging 
technologies will capture high- resolution visual data of food 
being chewed within the o ral cavity. External mounting of the 
camera is preferable to avoid obstructions from food particles 
sticking to the lens . When the chewing robot is in operation, 
there is only a brief time frame to capture these images since the 
occlusion phase and the opening and closing phases can obstruct 
the view of the food items. Hence, image capture must coincide 
with the fully open oral cavity phase to ensure clear visibility. 
Thus, the system must be synchronized with the chewing robot.

Compact cameras are ideal due to limited space and large 
mechanical components, allowing for flexible installation 
without compromising image quality. Given the possible 
obstructed view in the limited-space oral cavity, increasing the 
number of cameras, ideally positioned from two sides of the 
cavity, will  enhance the field of view, allowing for a more 
comprehensive evaluation of the textural properties of the 
chewed food. High resolution is essential for detailed visuals, 
enabling precise analysis of food texture and structural changes. 
A high frame rate ensures smooth, continuous video capture of 
every mastication phase. Proper lighting is vital, with polarized 
or diffuse lighting to minimize reflections from saliva. Cameras 
need a suitable focus range, with autofocus or motorized focus 
capabilities to maintain sharp images of moving objects. 
Additionally, compatibility with the robotic program and data 
processing software is also essential.  
Considering these factors, 2 endoscope cameras with built-
in lighting were selected as the most suitable for this scenario. 
These 5MP autofocus cameras, with a focal length starting from 
2 cm, will be strategically placed on both sides of the oral cavity

IV. IMAGE PROCESSING 
Images captured by the vision system must be transmitted in 
real time to a high -speed processing unit. This setup should 
minimize latency and ensure uninterrupted data flow, crucial for 
real-time analysis and prediction. High bandwidth requirements 
are managed through optimized data compression algorithms, 
preserving visual integrity while reducing data load. To enhance 
the efficiency and accuracy of the vision system, the region of 
interest (ROI) in the captured images needs to be carefully 
defined, as the  chewed food items will occupy only a small 
portion of the image. Training a machine learning model to 
detect and segment the chewed food will be effective, especially 
given the availability to gather a large dataset by the chewing 
robot. Hence, a proper model needs to be selected.   
Originally designed for medical image segmentation, U-Net 
is particularly well-suited for tasks requiring precise localization 
and has been widely adopted in medical imaging [11 ]. Using 
pure CNNs for object detection is costly, especially with varying 
object sizes. Region-based Convolutional Neural Networks (R-
CNNs) are more effective, performing a selective search to 
extract numerous region proposals from images [12]. Moreover, 
Fast R -CNN improves speed by passing the entire image 
through a CNN to generate ROIs but remains slow for large 
datasets. Faster R-CNN addresses this by allowing the network 
to learn region proposals directly, eliminating selective search  
[13]. Another model, Mask R-CNN extends the Faster R-CNN 
by adding a branch for predicting segmentation masks on each 
ROI, enabling precise pixel -wise segmentation and 
classification, which is ideal for dynamic environments. Figure 
3 visually shows semantic, instance, and panoptic 
segmentations. Thereby, U-Net makes it a sufficient choice for 
semantic segmentation of the food bolus in the complex visual 
environment.

Another model, Mask R-CNN extends the Faster R-CNN

Additionally, DeepLabv3+, is an advanced semantic 
segmentation model which uses an atrous convolution to capture 
multi-scale context by adopting image-level features [14]. These 
features are particularly useful in segmenting small or detailed 
objects such as pieces of food in varying textures and conditions.

Further, EfficientNet and EfficientDet provide a highly 
scalable and efficient framework for both image classification 
and object detection [15, 16]. These models are known for their 
superior performance and smaller model size, which is 
advantageous for real -time applications requiring rapid

segmentation of food bolus in in vitro chewing simulations. 
Their selection can be tailored based on specific requirements 
such as computational resources, latency constraints, and the 
specific characteristics of the visual data. 
V. DEEP LEARNING MODEL 
This model focuses on the integration and analysis of diverse 
inputs to predict the number of required chewing cycles to 
achieve a safe swallow food bolus in in vitro chewing 
simulations. These inputs can be mainly categorized into two 
distinct types as time-invariant and time-variant. Time-invariant 
inputs include several constant factors throughout the chewing 
process: 
• Chewing Trajectory 
• Saliva Rate 
• Food Hardness and Density 
• Force Applied 
Time-variant inputs provide dynamic data that changes 
throughout the chewing process:  
• Image textural features derived  from Gray Level Co -
occurrence Matrix (GLCM) of the image  help monitor 
the textural evolution of the food bolus, reflecting its 
status at various stages of mastication [17] 
• Moisture of the Bolus which influence cohesiveness 
• Size and number of chewed bolus particles 
To effectively manage and analyze the complex data derived 
from these inputs, the integration of a machine vision system 
coupled with a robust deep learning model is essential. The 
machine vision system plays a critical role in capturing real -
time, high-resolution images of the chewing process.

challenges. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) facilitate

Each deep learning model offers distinct advantages and 
challenges. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) facilitate 
sequential data processing through looped connections, though 
they risk information loss over long sequences. Long Short -
Term Memory (LSTM) unit s address this with cell states that 
selectively remember crucial details, but their sequential nature 
limits parallel processing and they do not explicitly model range 
dependencies. Attention mechanisms enhance focus on specific 
data subsets, improving model specificity but prohibiting 
parallel processing, which can slow operations on large datasets. 
Additionally, CNNs can parallelize tasks and capturing local 
patterns effectively, but they sometimes struggle with long-
range dependencies. Whereas Transform ers excel in 
parallelization and managing long -range dependencies via a 
mixture of encoders, decoders, and self-attention models [18]. 
A. CNN-RNN Model 
Recent advancements in hybrid deep learning architectures 
have sparked significant interest in their potential for handling 
both time -variant and time -invariant inputs in complex 
predictive models. Here, several key studies that represent the 
integration of CNNs and RNNs are examined, showcasing their 
collaborative potential in different applications. Long- term 
Recurrent Convolutional Networks (LRCNs), which effectively 
combine CNNs for image feature extraction with LSTMs for 
sequence prediction, demonstrates the power of this architecture 
in tasks l ike video description and event recognition [ 19]. 
Another research has explored the inner workings of RNNs and 
demonstrated how they can be combined with CNNs to process 
sequential image data, providing insights into the interpretability 
and capabilities of such hybrid models [ 20]. Additionally, the 
application of CNNs extract ing frame-level features and 
aggregating these by RNNs over time are presented in [ 21].

Another research has explored the inner workings of RNNs and 
demonstrated how they can be combined with CNNs to process 
sequential image data, providing insights into the interpretability 
and capabilities of such hybrid models [ 20]. Additionally, the 
application of CNNs extract ing frame-level features and 
aggregating these by RNNs over time are presented in [ 21]. 
Furthermore, researchers have employed LSTMs to learn video 
representations from CNN features, highlighting how temporal 
dynamics in data can be captured by RNNs following initial 
feature extraction by CNNs [ 22]. These studies highlight the 
architecture's ability to manage spatial features through CNNs 
and sequence dynamics via RNNs, demonstrating its relevance 
for handling time-variant and invariant inputs. 
B. Transformer Model 
Latest developments in Transformer models have 
increasingly focused on enhancing their ability to efficiently 
handle both time -variant and invariant data. The architecture 
introduced in [ 23], uses self -attention mechanisms to process 
sequences of data, offering a substantial improvement over 
earlier sequence-to-sequence models by eliminating the need for 
recurrent layers. In another study, the Transformer model is 
adapted for image processing tasks by treating image patches as 
sequences, which could be anal ogous to treating changes of 
bolus data as sequential inputs [24]. Additionally, [25] presents 
a Transformer model that processes video data by applying a 
pure transformer architecture directly to sequences of image 
frames. The model has effectively managed both spatial and 
temporal dimensions by treating video frames as a sequence of 
tokens. Similarly, another study introduces a model featuring a 
space-time attention mechanism, enabling the Transformer to 
effectively integrate and learn from both spatial a nd temporal 
features in video data [26]. This capability makes it particularly 
adept at monitoring dynamic changes in image properties over 
time, such as tracking the evolution of bolus characteristics 
during chewing. Hence, transformer models, excel in managing 
sequences with complex interactions.

VI. DISCUSSION 
The proposed conceptual model is to estimate the in vitro 
chewing cycles necessary for achieving a safe bolus formation, 
guided by time -variant parameters. Th e model with  real-time 
predictions will be a milestone not only for  in vitro chewing 
robotics research, but also for food manufacturers. Current 
challenges in food analysis include inconsistent and subjective 
results from human-based surveys. Furthermore, the analysis on 
food behavior during in vitro oral processing limits our 
understanding of food breakdown and interaction with saliva, 
creating potential gaps in real time analysis and for prediction 
models.  
Using a chewing robot equipped with artificial intelligence 
addresses these issues by providing accurate predictions on 
chewing behavior and changes in textural properties. It will 
allow detailed analysis of oral processing, examining how food 
breaks down and mixes with saliva, thereby ensuring food 
behaves as anticipated. This technology will also enable rapid 
analysis of large volumes of data with increased efficiency, 
providing valuable insights for food manufacturers. This 
integration of mechanical simu lation and advanced deep 
learning models will offer a comprehensive solution to these 
challenges, paving the way for more reliable and detailed food 
analysis and oral product development. 
VII. CONCLUSION 
This study presents a framework for a real -time deep 
learning model to estimate additional invitro chewing cycles for 
safe bolus formation, integrating a chewing robot, a vision 
system, an advanced image processing technique, and a deep 
learning model for prediction. The comparative analysis of 
CNN-RNN and transformer models underscores the potential of 
deep learning in enhancing our understanding of the chewing 
process. Future research may focus on the implementation and 
validation of this framework in rea l-world scenarios, with 
particular attention to the optimization of model performance 
and computational efficiency.

ABSTRACT In the context of food science and engineering, the in vitro chewing effect on food bolus
formation is a critical area of research that explores the mechanical and textural properties of ingested
materials. This article presents a pioneering approach to assess the in vitro chewing impact on food bolus
formation using the gray level co-occurrence matrix (GLCM) image analysis technique. As technological
advancements lead to the development of mastication robots, the need for evaluating in vitro chewed food
bolus has grown. To address this challenge, a case study is conducted. The study’s objectives encompass
utilizing GLCM to determine the in vitro chewing cycle phase, analyzing texture features, and investigating
chewing trajectory differences for beef and plant-based burger patties.

entropy, and variance are labeled as edge textures, having
high values when visual edges are present in the neighbor-
ing pixels. Alternatively, texture features labeled as interior
textures have high values for a neighborhood, which contains
few coherent edges but has many subtle and irregular varia-
tions.

Abstract— Recent technological advances have opened new 
ways to colorize grayscale images automatically, using different 
deep-learning techniques. Automatic colorization plays a 
crucial role in various applications such as coloring low -light or 
night vision images, historical photo restoration, for lights -out 
factories, medical imaging, and many more. Storing images in 
grayscale format significantly reduces storage requirements, 
making it an efficient solution for media storage and 
transmission, such as in CCTV footage, where grayscale can 
save up to two-thirds of storage space compared to color. 
Hence, grayscale image colorization has far more importance 
than anticipated. Colorization techniques were studied through 
an extensive literature review. Then, error calculations of 
colorized images were compared and analyzed. Progressively, 
different parameters which affect the colonization were 
changed and compared as hyperparameter tuning. Building 
upon this knowledge, an improved algorithm using a fusion -
based approach was developed. The algorithm concatenates 
local and global features of the image for plausible colorization 
results. The model was validated by using different images and 
is quantitively as well as qualitatively compared. Seven types of 
error calculation methods are used in this paper for comparison 
of the original and the predicted images. Furthermore, due to 
the lack of quantitative visual representation for the accuracy 
analysis of colorized images, a new concept of error analysis 
using heat maps are proposed.

C. Error Analysis 
In the context of error analysis, several studies have relied 
on human validation to assess the accuracy of colorization 
processes [18], [22]. In contrast to human validation methods, 
automated assessments tend to have discrepancies. The results 
from [12] and [20] appear desaturated, attributed to loss

automatically recognized by deep learning models through 
architectural design and training. Local features include 
distinct mountain peaks, clouds, trees, and fine details such as 
edges, contours, and internal textures of leaves, grass, or 
flowers. Hence, to improve basic AE algorithm, a new 
approach combines a convolutional autoencoder with a merge

for automatic colorization of greyscale images through a 
deep-learning fusion technique. The Average Error

models, this is achieved by minimum computational 
requirements. Additionally, this level of accuracy and 
plausible colorized pictures were predicted from just 346 
images for 200 epochs. Moreover, visual comparisons reveal 
the Improved Algorithm produces superior colorization, 
minimizing patches and staying within image feature 
boundaries. Moreover, a new quantitative technique using 
heat maps is proposed to visually illustrate errors in predicted 
images across various AI models.

2. Background 
Chewing robots represent a growing research area aimed at developing biomimetic oral cav- 
ities. Several robots such as the Tri-chewer [ 8 ], iBOMS-III [ 9 ], and 6-axis bionic chewing robot 
[ 10 ] have been engineered to match human mastication. In particular, the three-linked chew- 
ing robot known as ChewBot, was designed to reproduce molar trajectories, salivary action, 
force proﬁles and bolus repositioning within the oral cavity [ 3 ]. With these mechanical sys- 
tems now available, current effort s f ocus on replicating human-like bolus formation. Captur- 
ing high-resolution images of in vitro chewed boluses at each cycle is critical for characteriz- 
ing chewing behaviour and progression. However, the current lack of publicly available datasets 
hinders research progress in this area. To address this gap, we present the Invitro dataset un- 
der the ChewNet dataset [ 4 ] a ﬁrst-of-its-kind multimodal dataset. The Invitro dataset includes 
two food substrates plant-based and beef burger patties processed through sequential chewing 
cycles ranging from 1 to 40. For each cycle, we collected bolus images and force proﬁles, and 
at ﬁve-cycle intervals we recorded textural measurements. Along with Invitro dataset, ChewNet 
contains an Invivo experimental dataset which includes images of food boluses at the swal- 
lowing stage and it’s corresponding TPA measurements. The purpose of this whole multimodal 
dataset is to enable development of deep learning models to evaluate chewing dynamics and 
forecast subsequent chewing patterns, offering a synchronized visual, mechanical and textural 
record of bolus formation in a human analogous oral environment.

4.5. Biomimicking chewing robot 
Invitro chewed food boluses were collected using the biomimicking chewing robot, ChewBot 
which has 3-DOF (degree-of-freedom) equipped with a soft robotic oral cavity [ 3 ]. The chewing

increasing lateral displacement during occlusion, which result in greater shearing effect. T1 or 
the ﬁrst trajectory is more of a vertical motion with more focus on biting and compression. T13

robotic oral cavity provides the function of containing the food and repositioning it back be-

into the robot’s oral cavity is controlled by an automatic syringe to achieve a user-speciﬁed in- 
jecting rate.

Abstract— This paper presents a study on the evaluation of 
moisture content in in vitro chewed food boluses using image 
processing techniques.  Th is integration offers a novel, non -
destructive method that enhances the accuracy and efficiency of 
moisture assessments compared to traditional gravimetric 
methods and external sensors, which are typically more time-
consuming and potentially alter the sample’s properties.  Invitro 
food samples were taken for moisture analysis from a biomimetic 
robot equipped with automatic saliva injections. Image skewness, 
variance, lightness, and Gray -Level Co -occurrence Matrix 
(GLCM) analysis were found to quantitatively indicate moisture 
content for two types of in vitro chewed food samples, at different 
chewing cycles and trajectories . This pilot study was conducted 
with two food samples, but the approach can be applied to a 
broader range. The study's findings highlight the effectiveness of 
image processing in analyzing moisture dynamics within chewed 
food boluses, providing valuable insights that could enhance the 
design and functionality of biomimetic chewing robots to resemble 
human oral processing more closely.

I. INTRODUCTION 
During oral processing of food , the amount of m oisture 
varies due to saliva secretions. In humans, saliva content differs 
in food types , with an average retention of  approximately 
30wt% [1]. This suggests that a significant portion of the 
moisture content in chewed food is contributed by saliva 
indicating the pivotal role of moisture. Moisture plays a crucial 
role in oral processing of food influencing bolus texture, ease of 
swallowing, and its digestibility [2]. In vitro studies of chewed 
food boluses provide crucial insights into the mastication 
process. By incorporating saliva or saliva substitutes into food 
samples, these studies aim to closely replicate the human 
chewing experience. Recent advancements in robotic chewing 
devices have enhanced simulations of human mastication 
highlighting the need to evaluate chewed food boluses to closely 
mimic human oral processing [3] [4]. 
Computer vision has been widely applied in various food 
related analyses such as meat adulteration detection [5] and food 
industrial applications [6]. Food moisture content analysis using 
image processing have been primarily done for d ehydration 
processes [7] [8] [9]. Moreover, color features such as mean and 
standard deviation, have been extracted from two color spaces  
and moisture content of meat samples by chemical analysis for 
correlating color and moisture using partial least square 
regression (PLSR) model and a neural network (NN)  [10]. 
Hence, moisture analysis of in vitro chewed food boluses is a  
novel area of research. In contrast, moisture analysis for soil 
using image processing has been extensively studied  [11]. 
Various methods have been employed to determine moisture 
levels, analyzing changes in soil color [12], measuring intensity 
of iron ore pellet images [13], and utilizing descriptive statistics 
from different color channels of soil images [14].

moisture levels can also be signi fied using color changes as 
samples with higher moisture often appear in lighter shades. 
These visual attributes, such as edge curvature, smoothness, and

Variance in an image measures the spread or dispersion of pixel 
intensity values in a specific area  by the formula

there is less difference between them. This uniformity typically 
indicates smoothness because the area lacks significant texture 
or rapid changes in intensity, whic h would otherwise increase

there are significant fluctuations in pixel intensity. Hence, 
variance can be taken to measure smoothness. Several studies 
have introduced descriptors for measurin g image smoothness

variance to measure smoothness in in-vitro chewed food boluses 
is a relatively novel approach.

B. Calculate Lightness 
Lightness in an image refers to the brightness or luminosity 
of the colors within the image. In image processing, lightness is 
a crucial attribute for analysis. In the specific context of 
analyzing in-vitro chewed food bolus pictures, lightness can be 
particularly useful in assessing moisture content. Moisture in 
food affects its lightness because wetter surfaces tend to reflect 
light differently compared to drier ones. By analyzing the 
lightness values of images of chewed food bolus, researchers 
can estimate the moisture content of the food. The lightness of 
an image is calculated using the L component, which is derived 
by converting the image to the LAB color space. 
C. Calculate Skewness 
Skewness measures the asymmetry of pixel intensity 
distribution within an image. In the context of in vitro chewed 
food bolus images, skewness can be used to assess moisture 
content because it quantifies the asymmetry in pixel intensity 
distribution, with changes in skewness reflecting variations in 
texture and consistency due to moisture levels. The skewness of 
all images was calculated using the SciPy library.

IV. RESULTS 
This section presents the outcomes of the analyses 
performed to investigate moisture content using various image 
processing techniques, specifically focusing on variance, 
lightness, skewness, and the GLCM.  
A. Finding moisture using variance 
The analysis demonstrates a clear relationship between 
image variance and moisture content in both beef and plant 
patties. The results depicted in Figure 4 clearly illustrate that as 
moisture increases, the variance in pixel intensity across the 
images consistently decreases, indicating more uniform pixel 
values. This uniformity suggests that the areas with higher 
moisture content are smoother with less text ural variability. 
These findings support the hypothesis that variance can serve as 
a reliable indicator of moisture levels in chewed food boluses, 
providing a quantitative measure of smoothness that correlates 
with moisture content. These results contribute to the novel 
application of variance-based methods for assessing food bolus 
texture in a moisture-dependent context.

V. DISCUSSION 
This study demonstrated the use of image processing 
techniques in quantifying moisture content in chewed food 
boluses, highlighting their potential to provide rapid and non-
invasive assessments. The application of variance, lightness, 
skewness, GLCM features has captured the moisture variations 
within the boluses proving to be reliable indicators.  The 
significant findings from these four image processing techniques 
suggests  that these metrics are particularly responsive to 
changes in moisture content Hence, they provide a robust 
framework for ongoing in vitro chewed food bolus assessments. 
While each condition in this study was tested three times, the 
focus of this pilot study was primarily on exploring the 
feasibility of using image processing techniques for moisture 
assessment in in vitro chewed food boluses.  A more 
comprehensive statistical analysis, along with a broader range of 
food samples and additional testing conditions, can be explored 
in future research.

 A B S T R A C T
Non-invasive, continuous monitoring of food bolus transformation during robotic mastication remains a 
significant challenge, as existing methods rely on physical extraction of the bolus or single-modality image 
features that lack robustness across the continuous and non-linear nature of food breakdown. This paper 
investigates whether hybrid machine-extracted image features can reliably classify chewing phases during in 
vitro robotic mastication without physical intervention. A hybrid feature-extraction framework is proposed 
that integrates deep convolutional features from VGG16 with classical texture descriptors, Grey-Level Co-
occurrence Matrix (GLCM), image lightness, and variance, applied to a dataset of 1024 segmented chewed 
biscuit bolus images captured across two chewing trajectories: vertical motion (T1) and combined vertical and 
lateral motion (T13). Supervised classifiers, Support Vector Machines, Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA), and 
Random Forests were evaluated using trial-level grouped cross-validation. Using a 3-phase schema conceptually 
aligned with the Hutchings and Lillford Mouth Process Model, LDA achieved accuracies of 75.9% for T1 
and 82.3% (T13), with the hybrid feature set outperforming the ablation study. Improved separability with 
T13 demonstrates that shear effect produces more distinctive bolus image features.

structural interpretation. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), with 
their ability to learn hierarchical representations, have become central 
to estimating the mastication phases of human chewed food boluses 
(Nishi et al., 2019). In a recent study, deep learning-based segmentation 
techniques such as Mask R-CNN were successfully applied to analyse 
food bolus formation and particle changes during in vitro chewing, 
demonstrating the feasibility of real-time, non-invasive monitoring of 
dynamic texture changes (Ren et al., 2025). Beyond food applica-
tions, computer vision frameworks integrating GLCM-based features, 
statistical descriptors, Hough transform features, and feature-reduction 
techniques have demonstrated robust performance in challenging envi-
ronmental conditions, with optimised feature subsets achieving high 
detection accuracy using Support Vector Machines (SVM) (Li et al., 
2017). CNN models pre-trained on large datasets (e.g., ImageNet) 
such as VGG19, ResNet50, and Inception-based architectures have 
been adapted via transfer learning for food image recognition and 
classification tasks, showing effective performance in discriminating 
food categories and features in diverse food image datasets (Bu et al., 
2024). VGG-16 has achieved very high accuracy in classifying rice 
varieties based on colour and texture features, using a customised 
model with additional fully connected layers (Ishaq et al., 2025). Fur-
thermore, studies indicate that combining VGG16 features with SVM 
often outperforms VGG16 with SoftMax classifiers for texture analysis 
(Priya et al., 2021). Extending in this line of research, Hassan et al. 
(2025) proposes a novel hybrid deep learning model that integrates 
automated deep features with statistical textural descriptors (GLCM) for 
the classification of 3 Neurological disorders from Magnetic Resonance

Grounded in the Hutchings and Lillford Mouth Process Model 
(Hutchings and Lillford, 1988), which describes oral processing as a 
progressive and continuous transformation involving structural break-

framework and uses chew-count-based experimental stages to repre-
sent bolus transformation during robotic mastication. Specifically, the 
bolus images are classified into four neutral chewing-stage categories: 
unchewed state, initial, mid, and final chews, corresponding to 0, 1–5, 
6–10, and 11–15 chewing cycles, respectively. The novelty of this study 
lies in the engineering integration of robotic mastication, cycle-based 
image acquisition, and machine vision-based classification for moni-
toring bolus transformation. This paper proposes a feature-extraction 
framework that integrates deep convolutional features from VGG16 
with classical descriptors, including GLCM, lightness, and variance, 
to classify chew-count-based stages of in vitro mastication across two 
chewing trajectories. The primary classification scheme comprises three 
chewing phases and additionally a finer four-class partition based on 
equal-interval chew-count groupings is examined as an exploratory 
benchmark to probe the limits of image-based phase discrimination at 
higher resolution.

2. Methodology
2.1. Vision system
The experiments to generate food bolus were performed using a 
biomimetic masticating robot with a three-degree-of-freedom (DOF) 
linkage mechanism with an artificial cavity (Chen et al., 2022). The 
overall experimental setup and the robotic chewing system are illus-
trated in Fig.  1. The imaging setup consists of a Raspberry Pi HQ cam-
era. It captures images at a resolution of 2.1 megapixels (1920 × 1080 
pixels). Given the camera-to-bolus distance of approximately 10 cm 
and the 6 mm lens configuration, the effective field of view covering 
the oral cavity region is approximately 30–35 mm in width, yielding 
a spatial resolution of approximately 0.016–0.018 mm per pixel. This 
spatial resolution is appropriate for capturing bolus structural changes, 
which typically occur at millimetre to sub-millimetre scales in in-
vitro oral processing studies (Marconati and Ramaioli, 2020). The 
LED ring light strip operates under constant-current drive, providing 
stable illumination without flicker or significant thermal drift across the 
duration of each experimental trial. The camera and lighting assembly 
are rigidly fixed relative to the oral cavity, and all image frames are 
captured at the moment of maximum jaw opening, ensuring consistent 
geometric and illumination conditions across acquisitions (Akarawita 
et al., 2025). The vision system acquires high-quality images of the 
bolus as chewing progresses. This configuration supports the capture 
of fine-grained textural and structural variations associated with food 
breakdown.

2.2. Dataset description
The dataset consists of segmented images of food boluses generated 
during controlled robotic chewing experiments. Artificial saliva was 
replicated using an enzyme-active mouthwash (Oral7, 2025), intro-
duced at a controlled flow rate of 1 ml/min using a syring pump and a 
chewing rate of 3s. The use of such saliva substitutes has been explored 
in previous work to assess their role in altering the mineral content of 
dental enamel (Kielbassa et al., 2001). The robotic chewing platform 
enables precise and repeatable control of chewing parameters, ensuring 
consistency across trials and allowing systematic analysis of how dif-
ferent motion patterns influence particle fragmentation, size reduction, 
and bolus formation. A standardised food sample of 1 g biscuit (Maliban 
Biscuit Manufactories (Pvt) Ltd., 2026), as shown in Fig.  1, was selected 
due to its uniform initial structure and repeatability across trials. Two 
distinct chewing trajectories were examined to capture variations in 
chewing kinematics (Chen et al., 2022): Trajectory T1, which involves 
purely vertical motion and represents simple compression-based chew-
ing, and Trajectory T13, which combines vertical motion with shear 
forces to represent more complex grinding mastication patterns as 
shown in Fig.  2. For each trajectory, 512 images were collected across 
32 replicate chewing trials, each conducted with a fresh 1 g biscuit 
sample and a fully reset artificial saliva delivery system. Each trial 
contributed 16 images corresponding to the unchewed state and 15 
successive chewing cycles. Since each image originates from a distinct 
independent trial, the assumption underlying 5-fold grouped-stratified 
cross-validation is satisfied.

2.3.1. Deep learning features
Critically, image-based classification of food bolus transformation 
during in-vitro robotic mastication represents a novel and emerging 
research area, with very limited prior literature providing guidance 
on optimal deep learning backbone selection for this specific task. 
However, VGG16 was selected as a representative pretrained CNN and 
for several domain specific and practical reasons. First, its uniform 
stack of 3 × 3 convolutional filters captures fine-grained local texture 
patterns particularly effectively, unlike architectures such as ResNet 
or EfficientNet, whose residual connections and compound scaling are 
optimised for object-level semantic discrimination rather than low-
level texture encoding (Rani et al., 2025). Second, the fully connected 
layers of VGG16 produce a fixed 512-dimensional feature vector that 
is straightforward to concatenate with low-dimensional classical de-
scriptors (GLCM, lightness, variance), making it particularly compatible 
with the hybrid fusion pipeline employed here; by contrast, ResNet and 
EfficientNet require custom global average pooling strategies to yield 
equivalent fixed-length representations (Addisu et al., 2025).

2.3.2. Classical image features
To complement deep learning features, three categories of classical 
descriptors were extracted. First, texture properties were captured using 
GLCM analysis, computing three key metrics (Zubair and Alo, 2024): 
Energy, which reflects texture uniformity; Homogeneity, indicating the 
closeness of element distribution to the diagonal; and Dissimilarity, 
measuring variation between pixel pairs. Second, mean lightness values 
were derived from the L channel of the LAB colour space, providing in-
sights into overall brightness, which is a factor correlated with moisture 
content and particle size (Akarawita et al., 2024b). Finally, intensity 
variance was calculated to quantify texture heterogeneity, revealing 
the degree of particle size variation and mixing within the bolus. 
The extracted features were concatenated to form a 517-dimensional 
feature vector, as shown in Fig.  5. This fusion strategy combines 
the hierarchical representations from deep learning with interpretable 
texture descriptors from classical methods.
2.4. Feature normalisation and ablation study
Before classification, features were standardised using a Standard-
Scaler, which centres each feature to zero mean and scales it to unit 
variance across the dataset. This normalisation ensures that features 
from different sources and scales contribute equally to subsequent anal-
ysis. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was then applied to reduce 
dimensionality while retaining 95% of the total variance, reducing 
computational complexity and helping mitigate overfitting, particularly 
important when dealing with relatively small datasets (Bian et al., 
2022). Model evaluation was performed using trial-grouped stratified 
cross-validation, where all images originating from the same chew-
ing trial were assigned to the same fold. The overall methodology is 
represented as a flow chart in Fig.  6.

To evaluate the contribution of each feature group to classification 
performance, a formal ablation study was conducted comparing three 
feature configurations: (1) Classical-only, comprising GLCM energy, 
homogeneity and dissimilarity, mean lightness, and intensity variance 
(5-D); (2) VGG16-only, comprising the deep features extracted from the 
penultimate VGG16 layer (512-D); and (3) Full Hybrid, the concatena-
tion of both feature groups (517-D). Each configuration was processed 
and evaluated through the same pipeline. This controlled design en-
sures that observed accuracy differences are attributable solely to the 
feature content, not to differences in pipeline design or hyperparameter 
tuning.
2.5. Classification models
Classification of sequential or progressive phases is a common chal-
lenge in food science and robotics. Traditional machine learning ap-
proaches, including SVM, Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA), and 
Random Forest (RF) methods, have been successfully applied to food 
texture classification tasks (Jiménez-Carvelo et al., 2019). These three 
classifiers were selected to represent a complementary range of decision 
boundary strategies: linear (LDA), kernel-based (SVM), and ensemble 
tree-based (RF), which is a standard practice in machine learning 
benchmarks for multi-class image classification problems involving 
high-dimensional features (Syarief and Setiawan, 2020).
2.6. Hyperparameter tuning
To ensure a fair and rigorous comparison across classifiers and ker-
nel functions, hyperparameters for SVM, LDA, and RF were tuned using 
a systematic nested cross-validation strategy. An inner 5-fold strati-
fied grouped cross-validation loop was applied within the full hybrid 
feature space (517-D) to search over the predefined hyperparameter 
grid. The configuration yielding the highest mean inner-validation 
accuracy was selected and then evaluated on the held-out trial groups 
in the outer cross-validation loop. For SVM, three kernel functions 
were included in the search space simultaneously, ensuring that kernel 
selection itself was data-driven rather than assumed.

VI. DISCUSSION 
 The intermediate shafts are passed through the shell of 
the rod end ball bearings freely. Therefore, once the robot is 
in operation, the length of all the shafts will not be equal 
unless fixed. The intermediate shafts started to fall off the 
bearings and due to the shaft being passed into the bearings 
freely. Hence, intermediate shafts of 10mm diameter were 
taken and were threaded at the ends to a lesser diameter. By 
this, it was able to pass through the bearings freely and then 
they were tightened with a nut to achieve equal length.  
The initial decision was to undergo the manufacturing of 
links using carbon fiber due to its light weight and strength. 
Due to availability, cost, and fabrication, Aluminum was 
selected as the alternate material because of its lightweight 
and strength.  However, the material stress analysis, bending 
moment analysis and twist analysis done for each component 
for both carbon fiber and aluminum yielded well above the 
required value.  
Singularities were common at the initiation of the system.

withstand the acceleration of the system.
